fields.slideOutline:
スライド 1（表紙・スクロールを止める）
🐸
蛙始鳴
Frogs Begin to Sing

Japan's micro-season #19
May 5–9

スライド 2（72候とは）
Japan divides the year into
72 micro-seasons.

Each one lasts about 5 days.
Each one has a name.

This week's name:
"Frogs begin to sing."

スライド 3（なぜこの時期か）
In early May, farmers
flood the rice paddies.

Frogs have been waiting
underground for exactly
this moment.

They appear almost
immediately.

They've been doing this
for 10,000 years.

スライド 4（言葉遊び）
Frog = kaeru 蛙
Return home = kaeru 帰る

Same sound.
Different meaning.

Japanese people keep frog
figurines in their wallets —

to make money return.
to bring travelers home.

スライド 5（芭蕉の俳句）
The most famous haiku
ever written is about
a frog.

古池や 蛙飛び込む 水の音

An old silent pond.
A frog jumps in.
Splash. Silence again.

— Matsuo Bashō, 1686

スライド 6（今週できること）
This week:

Find still water after dark.
A canal. A pond. A puddle.

Listen.

The 72 micro-seasons aren't
just Japanese.

They're a way of paying
attention to right now.

fields.caption:
Last night at 10pm, the rice paddies turned on. 🐸

10,000 frogs. All at once.

Today marks micro-season #19 of Japan's ancient 72-season calendar: 蛙始鳴 — "Frogs begin to sing."

This is what happens when farmers flood the rice fields. Frogs that have been waiting underground all winter appear overnight, filling the countryside with sound that farmers have used as a planting signal for thousands of years.

The Japanese word for frog (kaeru 蛙) sounds identical to the word for "return home" (kaeru 帰る). So frog figurines are kept in wallets to make money return, and near doorways to bring travelers home safely.

Matsuo Bashō wrote the most famous haiku in Japanese history about a frog jumping into a pond. He was just paying attention.

That's all the 72 micro-seasons ask: pay attention to the texture of right now.

🔗 Full story in bio link — the sound, the paddies, and what Bashō was really listening to.
